column1: # Active Missions
There are currently 2 active craft on Mars: Curiosity rover (NASA), and Perseverance rover (NASA).

There are currently 7 active craft in orbit round Mars: Mars Odyssey (NASA), Mars Express (ESA), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (NASA), MAVEN (NASA), ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (ESA), Hope (MBRSC) and, Tianwen-1 (CNSA).

Space agencies currently active on Mars are:|- NASA: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (USA)|- ESA: European Space Agency|- MBRSC: Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre (UEA)|- CNSA: China National Space Administration
# Launch Windows
There's a low energy launch window for Mars every two years and two months (Earth time). There's also a minimum lowest energy cycle every 16 Earth years.
During the Nov 2013 launch window, 2 missions were launched: MAVEN (NASA), and Mars Orbiter Mission (ISRO).
During the March 2016 launch window, only 1 mission was launched: ExoMars TGO (NASA).
During the May 2018 launch window, only 1 mission was launched: InSight (NASA)
During the Jul-Sep 2020 launch window 3 missions were launched: Mars Hope orbiter (MBRSC), Tianwen-1 with the Zhurong rover (CNSA), and Mars 2020 Perseverance rover and Ingenuity helicopter (NASA).
There were no missions to Mars launched in the Aug-Nov 2022 launch window.
# Ingenuity
The Ingenuity helicopter (NASA) landed with the Perseverance rover. It made 72 flights with a cumulative airtime of 2hr 8min 55sec and covered a distance of more than 17 km.

The Ingenuity helicopter (NASA) achieved the first aerodynamic flight on another planet. To celebrate, it carries a piece from the Wright Flyer, and the location of it's first flight was named Wright Brothers Field.

The Ingenuity helicopter (NASA) was grounded after 72 flights when the wing tips were damaged. The area where it remains was renamed from Airfield Chi to Valinor Hills, a reference to the undying lands from Tolkien's "Lord of the Rings".
# Curiosity

The Curiosity rover is powered by a 4.8kg radioisotope pellet of plutonium-238 dioxide. This generates 100 watts of electricity and 2000 watts of heat that is used to warm Curiosity's outer components.

The Curiosity rover has patterned wheels to maintain traction. The pattern left in the sand is used by on-board cameras to estimate the distance traveled. The pattern is Morse code for "JPL" (.--- .--. .-..).

The Curiosity rover touched down in Gale Crater on August 6, 2012. The spot has been named Bradbury landing, for Ray Bradbury, author of Fahrenheit 451 and the Martian Chronicles who had died on June 5, 2012.
# Lander facts
The Zhurong rover (CNSA) operated for 347 sols (358 days) and travelled 1.92 km.
# Space Facts
The intensity of meteor showers is given as Zenithal Hourly Rate (ZHR). This is the number of meteors you would see under perfect conditions with the shower coming from directly overhead.
There are 88 constellations that are recognized by the International Astronomical Union (IAU). Unofficial patterns are knwon as Asterisms.
Over time, the tilt of the Earth rotates, this is called the axial precession. The equinoxes complete a full rotation every 26000 years.

It's coincidence that the winter solstice and perhelion (closest approach to the sun) are currently close together (21 Dec/2 Jan). Due to axial precession (a rotation of the Earth's tilt), apsis will move later through the year.

Time measured on a sundial can deviate by as much as +16m 30s (3 November), or -14m 6s (11 Feb). This is due to both obliquity (axial tilt) and eccentricity (oval orbit) which combine in the equation of time.
Accurate calculation of planetary locations needs to account for the change in velocity when travelling towards or away from the sun. However, they can be approximated using the Keplerian equations.

In Romance languages, days of the week are named after heavenly bodies in order of apparent speed in the sky: Solis (Sun), Lunae (Moon), Martis (Mars), Mercurii (Mercury), Jovis (Jupiter), Veneris (Venus), Saturni (Saturn).

In English, days are named for: Sun (Sun), Moon (Mon), Tyr (Tue), Odin (Wed), Thor (Thr), Frig (Fri), Saturn (Sat). Tue-Fri are Norse equivalents of the Roman Gods. Saturday retains the Roman name as the Norse just called it "washing-day" (laugardagr).
# Mars facts general
Mars orbits at a distance of between 1.3 to 1.6 AU, around 206 to 259 million km.
In Sanskrit the planet Mars is personified as the deity Mangala. He also goes by the title Lohita ('the red one'). Like his Roman counterpart, he presides over Tuesday.
The alchemical symbol for the planet Mars +SY:Mars+ is a stylised spear and shield representing Mars, the Roman god of war. It came to to represent the male gender through the works of Linnaeus.
Mars is the second smallest planet in the solar system after Mercury. Its mass is equivalent to 0.107 Earths and gravity is 38% of Earth.
Mars has a surface area that is 28.4% of Earth's, which is only slightly less than the amount of dry land on Earth (which is 29.2% of Earth's surface).
# Mars moons
Mars has two small moons named Phobos and Deimos. They are irregularly shaped and are thought to be captured asteroids.
Mars has two moons, Phobos and Deimos. They're 22km and 12km in diameter respectively. Both satellites were discovered in 1877 by Asaph Hall.

The larger of Mars's moons, Phobos has an orbital period of 7.6 hours. From the surface, Phobos rises in the west, sets in the east, and rises again in just 11 hours. It appears about a third of the size of Earth's moon.

The smaller of Mars's moons, Deimos, is just outside synchronous orbit (where the orbital period would match the planet's period of rotation). It rises in the east, but slowly, taking about 2.7 days to set. It appears slightly larger than Venus does from Earth.
The larger of Mars's moons, Phobos is named after the Greek god of panic, who is the son of Ares (Mars) and Aphrodite (Venus) and twin brother of Deimos.
The smaller of Mars's moons, Deimos is named after the Greek god of fear, who is the son of Ares (Mars) and Aphrodite (Venus) and twin brother of Phobos.
# Mars geography
The ice-filled Korolev crater near Mars's north pole is estimated to hold about 2,200km3.
The total elevation change of Olympus Mons from the northwest plains to its summit is almost 26km, roughly 3 times the height of Mount Everest.

Mars has no global magnetic field although localised pockets of magnetism are present. Due to its small size, the core has cooled rapidly halting the convective motions of liquid metals that generate a magnetic dynamo. The remaining magnetic field was then eroded by solar wind and cosmic radiation.
Mars is often called the "Red Planet" due to its reddish appearance, caused by iron oxide (rust) on its surface.
Mars has a thin atmosphere composed mainly of carbon dioxide (95.3%), with traces of nitrogen, argon, and other gases.
Mars is much colder than Earth, with average temperatures around -62 degrees Celsius.
Surface temperatures on Mars fluctuate between -70 and 0 degrees Celsius.
The Valles Marineris canyon system on Mars is one of the largest in the solar system, stretching about 4,000 kilometers long and reaching depths of up to 11 kilometers.
Mars has polar ice caps made of water and carbon dioxide. During the Martian winter, these caps expand as the carbon dioxide freezes out of the atmosphere.
The atmosphere on Mars is only about 1% as dense as Earth's atmosphere, which means there is less protection from harmful radiation and meteoroids.
Mars experiences massive dust storms that can engulf the entire planet and last for months. These storms can affect surface missions and obscure views from orbit.
Mars has trace amounts of methane in the atmosphere. As it breaks down relatively quickly, it could be  a sign of ongoing geological or biological activity, although its origin is still debated.
Mars has a rugged surface with numerous impact craters, volcanic features, and vast plains covered in dust and sand.
The Tharsis Bulge is a huge volcanic plateau on Mars that hosts some of the largest volcanoes in the solar system, including Olympus Mons.

Evidence of ancient river deltas and lakebeds suggests that liquid water once flowed on the surface of Mars billions of years ago. Minerals - including hematite, clay, and sulfates - support past water activity.
Mars has several deep trenches, such as Hebes Chasma and Hellas Planitia, formed by tectonic activity and volcanic processes.
Mars lost much of its atmosphere over billions of years, likely due to a combination of factors, including its smaller size and lack of a global magnetic field.
Mars bears the scars of ancient impact basins, such as Hellas and Argyre, which were formed by colossal asteroid or comet impacts early in its history.
Although Mars' volcanoes are currently dormant, evidence suggests that some may have been active relatively recently, geologically speaking.
Dust storms on Mars can affect its climate by absorbing and scattering sunlight, potentially influencing temperature and weather patterns.

The names of astrological mountains denote their structure:| - Mons: large, isolated, mountain.| - Tholus: small dome-shaped mountain or hill.| - Patera: dish-shaped depressions on volcano peaks.| - Dorsum: long low range (not present on Mars).
In most maps of Mars drawn before space exploration, the convention among astronomers was to put south at the top as the telescopic image of a planet is inverted.
The large Sinus Meridiani region (Meridian Bay) was used as the prime meridian by Beer and Madler in 1830. In 1972, the 500m Airy-0 crater was adopted as a more acurate reference point.
For general calculations, the prime meridian at Airy-0 is used; however missions will usually calculate relative to their landing point.
As the center of a 500m crater was insufficiently precise, the longitude of the Viking 1 lander at 47.95137° west is used as the reference point, this maintains Airy-0 as the prime meridian.
Planum Australe (the southern plain) was due to be explored by Mars Polar Lander (NASA), but it was lost during descent (3 Dec 1999)
Salty subglacial lakes in the southern polar regions are inferred from radar measurements but other hypotheses (saline ice, clay deposits) are also proposed.
Martian soil is toxic due to relatively high concentrations of chlorine and associated compounds, such as perchlorates, which are hazardous to all known forms of life.
# Mars calendars
A Mars sol is 24 hours, 39 minutes, and 35 seconds. A year is 687 sols, about 1 year and 320 days on Earth.
A Martian year is approximately 687 Earth days long, and a Martian day is called a "sol." Martian timekeeping is essential for coordinating missions and operations on the planet.

NASA uses the Mars Sol Date (MSD), a count of sols since the Julian date 29 Dec 1873 as a date prior to the 1877 perihelic opposition (when Mars is at its closest approach to the sun and aligned with Earth).

The Darian calendar uses the 'telescopic epoch' as year 0, approx 12 March 1609, as this was the year Johannes Kepler published "Astronomia Nova". It has the advantage that all historic observations of Mars occur in positive dates.
The Darian calendar has 24 months of 28 days each (except every 6th which has 27). The months are named for the constellations of the zodiac, alternately in Latin and Sanskrit.
The constellation of Sagittarius +SY:Sgr+ takes its name from the Latin for archer. The Sanskrit counterpart is Dhanus meaning bow. They are used as the 1st and 2nd months of the Darian calendar.

The constellation of Capricorn +SY:Cap+ takes its name from the Latin for goat's horn. The Sanskrit counterpart, Makara, refers to a sea-monster sometimes depicted as a crocodile. They are used as the 3rd and 4th months of the Darian calendar.

The constellation of Aquarius +SY:Aqr+ takes its name from the Latin for water-carrier. The Sanskrit counterpart is Kumbha, a type of pot used for water. They are used as the 5th and 6th months of the Darian calendar.

The constellation of Pisces +SY:Psc+ takes its name from the Latin for fish. The Sanskrit counterpart, Mina, has the same meaning. They are used as the names of the 7th and 8th months of the Darian calendar.

The constellation of Aries +SY:Ari+ takes its name from the Latin for ram. The Sanskrit counterpart is Mesha meaning sheep. They are used as the names of the 9th and 10th months of the Darian calendar.
The constellation of Taurus +SY:Tau+ takes its name from the Latin for bull. The Sanskrit counterpart, Rishabha, has the same meaning. They are used as the 11th and 12 months of the Darian calendar.
The constellation of Gemini +SY:Gem+ takes its name from the Latin for twins. The Sanskrit counterpart is Mithuna meaning paired. They are used as the 13th and 14th months of the Darian calendar.
The constellation of Cancer +SY:Cnc+ takes its name from the Latin for crab. The Sanskrit counterpart, Karka, has the same meaning. They are used as the 15th and 16th months of the Darian calendar.
The constellation of Leo +SY:Leo+ takes its name from the Latin for lion. The Sanskrit counterpart, Simha, has the same meaning. They are used as the 17th and 18th months of the Darian calendar.
The constellation of Virgo +SY:Vir+ takes its name from the Latin for maiden. The Sanskrit counterpart, Kanya, has the same meaning. They are used as the 19th and 20th months of the Darian calendar.
The constellation of Libra +SY:Lib+ takes its name from the Latin for scales. The Sanskrit counterpart, Tula, has the same meaning. They are used as the 21st and 22nd months of the Darian calendar.

The constellation of Scorpius +SY:Sco+ takes its name from the Latin for scorpion. The Sanskrit counterpart, Vrishika, has the same meaning. They are used as the 23rd and 24th months of the Darian calendar.
The Darian calendar uses a variation on the latin weekdays; Lunae (Moon), Martis (Mars), Mercurii (Mercury), Jovis (Jupiter), Veneris (Venus), Saturni (Saturn), Solis (Sun).
